The field of AI is littered with overlapping buzzwords—AI, ML, deep learning, generative AI—and it is easy to lose track of how they relate.
Here is the precise hierarchy.
Artificial Intelligence is the broadest umbrella term, encompassing any machine that behaves remotely like a human or exhibits some form of intelligence [c331].
Inside that umbrella sits Machine Learning, a subset of AI where machines learn and adapt based on how users interact with them [c332].
Inside ML sits Deep Learning, which specifically involves neural networks—whereas ML also encompasses other approaches like decision trees [c333].

sentences.text: LLMs are a subset of deep learning that deal exclusively with text and do not involve images [c338].
That last qualifier is important: the moment you add images, audio, or video to the mix, you have crossed into a different (though related) territory.
That related territory is Generative AI—a mixture of large language models and deep learning that deals with multiple modalities including text, images, sound, and video [c339].
Generative AI uses deep neural networks to create new content such as text, images, and various forms of media [c340].
So while every LLM is a piece of deep learning, not every piece of generative AI is an LLM.

Pre-training means training an LLM on a huge amount of data so that it can perform a wide range of tasks [c23].
The key word is *huge*.
We are not talking about thousands or even millions of examples—we are talking about hundreds of billions of tokens of text scraped from the internet and other sources.

Two prominent sources illustrate the scale:

The training objective during pre-training is deceptively simple: next-word prediction.

sentences.text: For now, it is enough to know that the transformer's power comes from a mechanism called **attention**.
The attention mechanism is the core component of the transformer architecture that makes it powerful [c3710].
Intuitively, attention allows the model to decide which parts of the input are most relevant when producing each part of the output.
More precisely, the attention mechanism gives LLMs selective access to the entire input sequence when generating output one word at a time [c3711].
The self-attention mechanism captures long-range dependencies in a sentence, allowing better prediction of the next word [c3355].
This is a crucial capability: in a long sentence, the word that best predicts the next word might be ten or twenty words back.
Earlier architectures struggled with this; transformers handle it naturally.
Several components work together to make attention function correctly:
**Attention scores** are a key component of the attention mechanism [c3667].

One of the most striking capabilities of large pre-trained language models is their ability to perform tasks they were never explicitly trained on.
This phenomenon has two related names depending on how much task-specific information the model is given at inference time.
**Zero-shot learning** is the ability to generalize to completely unseen tasks without any prior specific examples [c3372].
In zero-shot learning, the model predicts the answer given only a description of the task with no supporting examples [c3374].
For instance, in zero-shot translation, the model is given only the task description "translate English to French" and the input word "breakfast" without any translation examples [c3385].
The model is completing tasks without any examples at all [c3387].
sentences.reason: c3387 states zero-shot learning is completing tasks without any examples.

sentences.text: **Few-shot learning** is learning from a minimum number of examples which the user provides as input [c3373].
In few-shot learning, the model is provided with a few supplementary examples to perform a task [c3440].
The model sees a few examples of a task to learn from [c3378], and these examples are provided directly in the input prompt rather than through any weight update [c3388].

sentences.text: Between these two extremes sits **one-shot learning**, where the model sees a single example of the task in addition to the task description [c3376].
